title: Self-Attention — 7 Learning Questions
subtitle: Topic: Self-Attention and Contextual Representation Learning · Subject: Transformers and LLM Architecture. Seven exact questions with only leading Layer labels omitted, balanced A–D choices and seven distinct SVG teaching scenes.
hero:
SELF-ATTENTION · VISUAL OVERVIEW

Every token can use context from other tokens

One token forms a query, compares against visible keys, then gathers a weighted mixture of their values. Context changes its representation.

questions.stem: What is Self-Attention in Artificial Intelligence, and how does it allow each word or token in a sequence to gather information from other tokens within the same sequence?
questions.figure:
TOKEN RELATIONSHIP CONSTELLATION

Each word gathers information through learned attention links

Visual takeaway: Each query token gets its own distribution of attention weights. A token is not forced to treat every other token equally.
options: Self-attention passes each token unchanged through the model without consulting surrounding words.
Self-attention lets each token combine information from other tokens in its sequence.
Self-attention assigns fixed meanings to tokens before processing any surrounding sentence context.
Self-attention sorts sentence tokens alphabetically before combining their learned vector representations.
questions.explanation: Correct: B. Self-attention compares each token with tokens in the same sequence and uses learned weights to combine their information. This produces context-aware representations. Different attention masks decide which positions a token is allowed to see.

questions.stem: How does Self-Attention differ from traditional Attention Mechanisms and sequential processing methods such as RNNs and LSTMs, and why is it a fundamental building block of Transformer architectures?
questions.figure:
RNN CROSS ATTENTION AND SELF ATTENTION

Three mechanisms: recurrent state, cross-attention, self-attention

Key distinction: Self-attention derives Q, K and V from one sequence. RNNs propagate state step by step; cross-attention can compare one sequence against another.
options: It requires output tokens to attend only to information from a separate encoder.
It processes each token sequentially, storing context in a repeatedly updated hidden state.
It prevents tokens from interacting directly, relying on fixed-distance convolution filters instead.
It links tokens within one sequence, allowing Transformers to process them in parallel.
questions.explanation: Correct: D. Classic encoder-decoder attention may use queries from one sequence and keys/values from another. In self-attention, all three come from the same sequence. Unlike RNNs and LSTMs, Transformer self-attention can calculate positions together during training, while adding direct token-to-token interaction paths.

questions.stem: How does Self-Attention understand relationships between words in a sentence, such as determining what the word "it" refers to in "The animal crossed the road because it was frightened," and how does context influence the representation of each token?
questions.figure:
PRONOUN COREFERENCE ATTENTION SPOTLIGHT

Which noun does “it” refer to? Context guides the signal

Interpretation: A model may use “frightened” to favor “animal” over “road.” Attention alone is not a proof of model reasoning or a reliable explanation by itself.
options: Attention may connect it to animal when context suggests the animal was frightened.
It chooses road as the reference simply because that word appears closest in order.
It always links the pronoun to whichever noun appears first in the sentence.
It replaces the pronoun with a fixed dictionary meaning without considering nearby sentence context.
questions.explanation: Correct: A. In this sentence, 'frightened' makes 'animal' a plausible antecedent for 'it'. An attention head may assign more weight to the animal token as part of its contextual representation. Attention weights are learned and are not definitive explanations of linguistic reasoning; multiple heads and layers contribute.

questions.stem: How does Self-Attention mathematically transform input embeddings into Query (Q), Key (K), and Value (V) matrices, calculate token-to-token similarity scores, apply scaling and softmax normalization, and generate contextualized token representations using the formula \(\operatorname{softmax}(QK^T/\sqrt{d_k})V\)?
questions.figure:
QKV MATRIX MULTIPLICATION AND SOFTMAX

Scaled dot-product attention turns comparisons into weighted values

Math: Q=XWq, K=XWk, V=XWv. Use QKᵀ/√dₖ for scores, apply masks if needed, softmax each row, then multiply by V. Heatmap values are illustrative.
options: It computes token scores by adding embedding vectors, then selecting only the largest.
It computes token scores from Value vectors, then averages every row without normalization.
It projects Q, K, V; scales QKᵀ, softmaxes scores, and weights V.
It generates Q from positional indices only, then multiplies unnormalized scores by keys.
questions.explanation: Correct: C. From inputs X, learn projections Q=XWq, K=XWk, V=XWv. The similarity matrix QKᵀ compares each query with all keys; dividing by √dₖ prevents scores becoming too large. Row-wise softmax turns scores into weights, and multiplying by V produces contextualized vectors. Masks exclude forbidden positions before softmax.

questions.stem: How can a Self-Attention layer be implemented from scratch using Python and PyTorch, including learnable projection matrices, matrix multiplication, attention weight calculation, optional masking, and visualization of the resulting token-to-token attention matrix?
questions.figure:
PYTORCH QKV PROJECTION AND CAUSAL HEATMAP

Implement learned projections, optional masking, and attention weights

self_attention.py · PyTorch
import math, torch
from torch import nn

torch.manual_seed(7)
class SelfAttention(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, dim):
        super().__init__()
        self.q = nn.Linear(dim, dim, bias=False)
        self.k = nn.Linear(dim, dim, bias=False)
        self.v = nn.Linear(dim, dim, bias=False)

    def forward(self, x, causal=False):
        Q, K, V = self.q(x), self.k(x), self.v(x)
        scores = Q @ K.transpose(-2, -1)
        scores = scores / math.sqrt(K.shape[-1])
        if causal:
            n = x.size(-2)
            allowed = torch.ones(n, n, dtype=torch.bool, device=x.device).tril()
            scores = scores.masked_fill(~allowed, float("-inf"))
        weights = scores.softmax(dim=-1)
        return weights @ V, weights

x = torch.randn(1, 4, 8)
out, attention = SelfAttention(8)(x, causal=True)
print(out.shape, attention.shape)
print(attention[0].round(decimals=2))
Token-to-token attention

Heatmap is illustrative; the code prints its actual random-initialized weights.

Hands-on: The snippet creates Q/K/V with trainable matrices, calculates attention, and masks future positions when requested. No pretrained model is needed.
options: PyTorch generates attention by sorting token positions, without trainable projections or masking.
PyTorch projects input vectors, computes masked scores, applies softmax, and combines values.
PyTorch requires a pretrained language model because attention cannot use random initialization.
PyTorch replaces attention weights with constant probabilities independent of sequence content.
questions.explanation: Correct: B. A basic PyTorch implementation uses trainable nn.Linear projections for Q, K, and V, computes Q @ K.transpose(-2,-1) / √dₖ, optionally masks forbidden positions, normalizes with softmax and multiplies by V. The resulting matrix contains one attention distribution per query token.

questions.stem: How does Self-Attention behave differently in Bidirectional Transformers such as BERT and Causal Transformers such as GPT, including attention masks, information visibility, positional encoding, multi-head projections, and the influence of context length on token representations?
questions.figure:
BERT VERSUS GPT VISIBILITY HEATMAPS

Visibility matrices: full context or past-only context?

Architecture: Bidirectional attention can use both sides of a token in the input. Causal decoding forbids future tokens. Heads learn different projections, and longer context increases full-attention cost.
options: BERT blocks right-side context, while GPT always accesses future positions during training.
Both models use identical visibility masks, differing only in the output vocabulary size.
Neither model uses token positions, since attention scores already express token order.
BERT commonly sees both directions; GPT masks future positions during causal processing.
questions.explanation: Correct: D. A bidirectional encoder such as BERT usually allows a token to use both earlier and later input positions. A causal decoder such as GPT prevents attention to future tokens, preserving autoregressive prediction. Both rely on positional information and multiple attention heads; increasing context length increases the available information and attention cost.

questions.stem: How can Self-Attention be optimized for large-scale Transformer models, including reducing quadratic computational complexity, managing KV caches during autoregressive inference, applying FlashAttention and sparse attention patterns, and evaluating the trade-offs between memory usage, processing speed, and long-context information retrieval?
questions.figure:
FLASHATTENTION TILING KV CACHE AND SPARSITY

Long-context optimization: tiles, cache reuse, and sparse patterns

Trade-off: FlashAttention is exact full attention with less memory traffic, not a subquadratic algorithm. KV caching helps decoding, while sparse patterns reduce work but can miss relevant tokens.
options: Tiling saves attention memory traffic; caching reuses past keys and values during decoding.
FlashAttention removes all quadratic arithmetic, while KV caches reduce training memory to zero.
Sparse attention always preserves exact full attention, regardless of its selected pattern.
KV caches discard older tokens, so autoregressive decoding becomes independent of context.
questions.explanation: Correct: A. Ordinary full self-attention scores all token pairs, giving O(n²) score interactions. FlashAttention reorganizes exact attention into IO-efficient tiles, reducing memory traffic rather than eliminating quadratic arithmetic. KV caching reuses previous keys/values in causal inference. Sparse patterns reduce interactions but may miss distant dependencies. Evaluate speed, memory and retrieval quality together.
